noteBlocks.md: A **monomer** is a small molecule that can join to others like it; a **polymer** is the very long chain molecule made when thousands of them join. The process is **addition polymerisation**: *addition* because the monomers add on to one another and nothing else forms, *polymerisation* because a polymer results. The name is the same whatever the monomer, and each word earns a mark.

**Monomer, and not a monomer.** Fluoroethene, $\ce{CH2=CHF}$, is a monomer: its C=C lets it join on. Fluoroethane, $\ce{CH3CH2F}$, looks almost the same but is not one: every bond is single, so it has nothing to join with. A monomer for this process always has a C=C.

noteBlocks.stem: Fluoroethene, $\ce{CH2=CHF}$, forms a polymer, and no other product is made. Name the process. **[2]**

steps.working: The monomers add on to one another, and nothing else forms: **addition**.
steps.decision: Addition is the first word and the first mark: it says how they join, with no second product.

steps.working: One very long chain molecule, a polymer, is made: **polymerisation**.
steps.decision: Polymerisation is the second word and the second mark. Written on its own it earns only one of the two.

noteBlocks.prompt: Asked to name the process in which dichloroethene molecules join into a polymer, a student writes only: polymerisation. What does the answer lose?
options: the mark for addition: the name has two words, and each earns a mark
nothing: polymerisation is the full name
both marks: polymerisation is the name of a different process
noteBlocks.answer: the mark for addition: the name has two words, and each earns a mark
noteBlocks.explain: Steps 1 and 2 of See it earn one mark each: addition says the monomers add on with nothing else formed, and polymerisation says a polymer is made. Polymerisation on its own is half the name, so it keeps one mark and loses the other.

optionNotes.option: nothing: polymerisation is the full name
optionNotes.why: Polymerisation says a polymer forms but not how, and the scheme gives a separate mark for the word addition.

optionNotes.option: both marks: polymerisation is the name of a different process
optionNotes.why: Polymerisation is the right word, so it keeps its own mark; only the missing word addition costs one.

twin.prompt: Which word of the name addition polymerisation says that no other product is formed?
options: addition
polymerisation
monomer
twin.explain: Addition says the monomers simply add on to one another, so nothing else is made: step 1 of See it. Polymerisation only says that a polymer is the result.

optionNotes.option: polymerisation
optionNotes.why: Polymerisation says what is made, a polymer, not whether anything else is made with it.

optionNotes.option: monomer
optionNotes.why: Monomer is not part of the process's name at all; it is the small molecule that joins up.

noteBlocks.md: When one bond of a C=C opens, each of its two carbons gains a spare bond, and that spare bond links it to the next monomer. Only one of the two bonds opens, so the carbons of each monomer stay joined, now by a single bond. Nothing leaves: the chain holds every atom the monomers brought.

noteBlocks.title: Why nothing else is made
noteBlocks.md: No atom leaves when a bond opens, so no second product forms. Section 7 turns this into a check on every repeat unit you draw.

noteBlocks.stem: Three ethene molecules, $\ce{C2H4}$, join into a section of chain, as the picture at the top shows. Say what happens to the bonds, and count the atoms in the chain.

steps.working: One bond of each C=C opens, which leaves each carbon one spare bond.
steps.decision: Only one of the two bonds opens: the two carbons of each monomer stay joined.

steps.working: The spare bonds link the monomers: $3 \times 2 = 6$ carbons in a row, every bond between them single.
steps.decision: Each monomer brings its two carbons, so the chain grows two carbons at a time.

steps.working: Nothing leaves: $3 \times 4 = 12$ hydrogens, the same as in the three ethene molecules.
steps.decision: Counting the atoms before and after checks that nothing was lost.

noteBlocks.prompt: Fluoroethene molecules join into a chain in the same way. How are the chain's carbon atoms joined to each other?
options: by single bonds
by double bonds
they are not joined at all
noteBlocks.explain: Step 1 of See it: only one bond of each C=C opens, and the freed bond links the carbon to the next molecule, so every bond along the chain is one line. A carbon that kept its double bond and linked on as well would have five bonds.

optionNotes.option: by double bonds
optionNotes.why: The monomer had a double bond, so it is easy to think the chain keeps it, but one of its two bonds is what opened to link on.

optionNotes.option: they are not joined at all
optionNotes.why: Only one of the two bonds opens, so the carbons of each monomer stay joined, and the freed bonds join them to their neighbours too.

twin.prompt: In the chain, how many bonds does each carbon atom make in all?
options: four
three
five
twin.explain: Carbon always makes four bonds. A chain carbon has two to its neighbours in the chain and two to the groups it carries, which is why the bonds between chain carbons must be single.

optionNotes.option: three
optionNotes.why: Three counts only the two chain bonds and one group, but every chain carbon also carries a second group.

optionNotes.option: five
optionNotes.why: Five would mean the double bond was kept as well as the new link, and carbon never makes more than four bonds.

noteBlocks.md: An **alkane** has only single bonds, and every one is already in use joining carbon to carbon or carbon to hydrogen. With no bond to open, no carbon gains a spare bond, so an alkane **cannot** form an addition polymer. That is why every monomer here is an **alkene**, or has a C=C like one.

noteBlocks.stem: Hex-1-ene, $\ce{CH2=CHCH2CH2CH2CH3}$, can form an addition polymer, but hexane, $\ce{C6H14}$, cannot. Explain why. **[2]**

steps.working: Hex-1-ene has a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to the next molecule.
steps.decision: The first mark is the double bond and what it does: one bond opens, freeing a bond on each carbon.

steps.working: Hexane has only single bonds, all in use, so it has no bond to open.
steps.decision: The second mark is the other half: say what the alkane lacks, not only what the alkene has.

noteBlocks.prompt: Ethene and ethane both have two carbon atoms. Why can ethene form an addition polymer when ethane cannot?
options: ethene has a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to the next molecule
ethene has more hydrogen atoms to give away
ethane molecules are too large to join together
noteBlocks.answer: ethene has a C=C, and one of its two bonds can open to link to the next molecule
noteBlocks.explain: Compare them as steps 1 and 2 of See it compared hex-1-ene with hexane: ethene's carbons share two bonds, and opening one frees a bond on each carbon to link on. Ethane's bonds are all single and all in use. So the reason is the C=C that can open.

optionNotes.option: ethene has more hydrogen atoms to give away
optionNotes.why: Ethene has fewer hydrogens than ethane, not more, and no hydrogen leaves when the chain forms: the joining is done by the C=C.

optionNotes.option: ethane molecules are too large to join together
optionNotes.why: Both molecules have two carbons, so size is not the difference; ethane simply has no bond to open.

twin.prompt: Pent-2-ene can form an addition polymer, but pentane cannot. Why?
options: pent-2-ene has a C=C that can open to link to the next molecule; pentane has only single bonds
pentane has more hydrogen atoms to give away
pent-2-ene molecules are smaller than pentane molecules
twin.answer: pent-2-ene has a C=C that can open to link to the next molecule; pentane has only single bonds
twin.explain: The same two halves as See it: the alkene's C=C has a bond to open, and the alkane has none, because every bond is single and in use.

optionNotes.option: pentane has more hydrogen atoms to give away
optionNotes.why: No hydrogen leaves in addition polymerisation, so a spare hydrogen is no help; what joins the chain is the C=C.

optionNotes.option: pent-2-ene molecules are smaller than pentane molecules
optionNotes.why: Both have five carbons, so size is not the difference; only the alkene has a bond it can open.

noteBlocks.text: 4. Naming a polymer from its monomer

noteBlocks.md: Build the polymer's name from the monomer's: **poly**, then the monomer's name **in brackets**. Ethene gives **poly(ethene)**, also called polythene; chloroethene, sold as **PVC** for window frames and drainpipes, gives **poly(chloroethene)**. Asked to name a polymer, write the chemical name, not the trade name. Read backwards, the monomer is the name inside the brackets.

noteBlocks.stem: Name the polymer made from fluoroethene, $\ce{CH2=CHF}$. **[1]**

steps.working: The monomer's name, fluoroethene, goes inside the brackets.
steps.decision: The name comes from the monomer, never from what the chain looks like, so it never ends in -ethane.

steps.working: Write poly in front: **poly(fluoroethene)**.
steps.decision: Brackets round the monomer's name; polyfluoroethene, written without them, is also accepted.

noteBlocks.prompt: Name the polymer made from the monomer dichloroethene.
noteBlocks.explain: The rule of step 2 of See it works for any monomer: poly, then the monomer's name in brackets, so dichloroethene gives poly(dichloroethene). The chain has only single bonds, but the name still comes from the monomer, so it never ends in -ethane.

twin.prompt: A polymer is called poly(hex-1-ene). Name the monomer it was made from.
twin.explain: Read the rule backwards: the monomer is the name inside the brackets, hex-1-ene. It has the C=C, so it could polymerise; hexane could not.

noteBlocks.md: A polymer is too long to draw, so you draw one **repeat unit**: the part that repeats all along the chain. It shows the two carbons of the C=C joined by a **single** bond; every group each carbon had in the monomer, in the same place; a **bond through each square bracket**, because the chain carries on; and **n** after the closing bracket, because the unit repeats many times.

noteBlocks.stem: Draw the repeat unit of poly(fluoroethene), made from $\ce{CH2=CHF}$. **[2]**

steps.working: Find the C=C: its two carbons make the chain.
steps.decision: Only the carbons of the double bond gain a spare bond when it opens.

steps.working: Join them with a single bond: F and H on the first carbon, H and H on the second.
steps.decision: Copy every group across exactly; only the bond between the carbons changes.

steps.working: Add a bond through a square bracket on each side, and n after the closing bracket.
steps.decision: The bonds through the brackets show the chain carrying on; n shows the unit repeating.

noteBlocks.prompt: Working back from a section of polymer chain to its monomer, what is the last step?
options: put the C=C back between the two carbons of the unit
remove the bonds that join the unit to its neighbours
mark off two neighbouring carbons that repeat
noteBlocks.answer: put the C=C back between the two carbons of the unit
noteBlocks.explain: The order is mark off two carbons, remove the outer bonds, then put the double bond back: steps 1 to 3 of See it. The last step is the one most often left out, and without it the answer is an alkane, which could never have polymerised.

optionNotes.option: remove the bonds that join the unit to its neighbours
optionNotes.why: Removing the outer bonds comes second; stopping there leaves a molecule with no C=C, an alkane that could never have polymerised.

optionNotes.option: mark off two neighbouring carbons that repeat
optionNotes.why: Marking off the unit is where the method starts, not where it ends.

optionNotes.option: count every hydrogen in the chain

optionNotes.option: two

noteBlocks.prompt: Tetrafluoroethene, C₂F₄, has a C=C with two fluorine atoms on each carbon. What goes between the two carbons of its repeat unit?
options: a single bond, with two F on each carbon
a double bond, with two F on each carbon
a single bond, with one F on each carbon
noteBlocks.answer: a single bond, with two F on each carbon
noteBlocks.explain: The rule is the same for any monomer, as See it showed for chlorotrifluoroethene: one bond of the C=C opens, leaving a single bond, and every group stays where it was. Two F on each carbon in the monomer means two F on each carbon in the unit.

optionNotes.option: a double bond, with two F on each carbon
optionNotes.why: The groups are right, but keeping the double bond would give each carbon five bonds once the bonds through the brackets are drawn.

optionNotes.option: a single bond, with one F on each carbon
optionNotes.why: The bond is right, but two fluorines have gone missing, and no atom leaves when the monomers join.

twin.prompt: 1,1-Difluoroethene is CH₂=CF₂. What does the repeat unit of its polymer show on its two carbons?

two H on one carbon and two F on the other, joined by a double bond
twin.answer: two H on one carbon and two F on the other, joined by a single bond
twin.explain: Open the C=C to a single bond and copy each carbon's own groups: the carbon that had two H keeps them, and the one that had two F keeps those.

optionNotes.option: one H and one F on each carbon, joined by a single bond
optionNotes.why: The atoms are all there, but they have been moved: each carbon keeps exactly the groups it had in the monomer.

optionNotes.option: two H on one carbon and two F on the other, joined by a double bond
optionNotes.why: The groups are right, but the double bond is the one thing that must open when the chain forms.

noteBlocks.md:
Name the process, **addition polymerisation**, and any polymer: poly(monomer).
Draw a repeat unit: a **single** C–C bond, a bond through each **bracket**, **n**; n on both sides of the equation.
Check it: the **same atoms** as the monomer, four bonds at every carbon.
Work back from a chain to its monomer by putting the **C=C** back.
Keep side groups off the chain, whatever the monomer.

Polymers sit inside the organic question of the C2 paper. The first marks are names: the process, or the polymer from its monomer. At Higher the last marks are a drawing: a repeat unit, a structural equation with n on both sides, or a monomer from a section of chain. Stuck? Draw the monomer, open its double bond, count four bonds at every carbon. The Sheet lists the traps.

items.stem: What is the functional group of the alkenes?
items.skill: Prerequisite from c2-alkenes; you are not expected to have met polymers yet

options.feedback: The C=C. This lesson is about what happens when thousands of those double bonds open at once.
That is the alcohols' group. The alkenes' is the carbon-to-carbon double bond.
Every hydrocarbon has C–H bonds, so they cannot be what makes the alkenes different. The C=C is.

items.stem: How many covalent bonds does a carbon atom form in a stable molecule?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 covalent bonding and c2-homologous-series-alkanes

options.feedback: Four. Counting to four at every carbon is the check you will use on every repeat unit you draw.
Oxygen forms two. Carbon forms four, and a drawing where it has three or five is wrong.
It never changes, which is what makes it such a useful check on a drawing.

items.stem: Ethene reacts with bromine in an addition reaction. What happens to its double bond?

options.text: one of the two bonds opens, and an atom joins each carbon
options.feedback: That is addition. Polymerisation is the same move, except that the thing joining each carbon is the next ethene molecule.

options.text: both bonds break, and the molecule splits in two
options.feedback: The carbons stay joined, by a single bond. Only one of the two bonds opens.

options.text: a hydrogen atom is swapped for a bromine atom
options.feedback: That would be substitution, which leaves a second product. Addition makes one product and nothing else.

options.text: a very long chain molecule made when many monomers join together
options.feedback: Long chain, many monomers. Those are the two ideas a definition needs.

options.text: a small molecule with a double bond that can join to others
options.feedback: That is the monomer. The polymer is what thousands of them make.
A polymer is one kind of molecule, and it contains no C=C at all once it has formed.

options.text: a molecule with many double bonds
options.feedback: The double bonds are what opened to make the chain. A polymer made this way has only single bonds along it.

items.stem: Give the full name of the process that turns ethene into poly(ethene).

options.feedback: Both words, and both are marks.
Half the name, so half the marks. The scheme also wants the word addition.
Cracking breaks big molecules into smaller ones; this process joins small ones into a big one.
Fermentation makes ethanol from sugar. Joining monomers into a chain is addition polymerisation.

items.stem: Name the polymer made from ethene.
items.skill: Name a polymer from its monomer

options.feedback: Poly, then the monomer's name in brackets.
The chain has only single bonds, but the name still comes from the monomer, and the monomer is ethene.
Ethanol is an alcohol, not an alkene. The monomer here is ethene.
There is no chlorine in ethene. That name mixes up the two polymers CCEA names.

items.stem: Which of these molecules could be a monomer for an addition polymer?
items.skill: Recognise a monomer by its C=C

options.feedback: It has a C=C, so it can polymerise: its polymer is poly(propene).
An alkane: only single bonds, all in use, so nothing can open.
An alcohol with no C=C. Addition polymerisation needs a double bond to open.
One carbon and four single bonds: no double bond, so no way to join into a chain.

items.stem: In a drawn repeat unit, what passes through each bracket?
items.skill: The features of a repeat unit

options.text: a bond, showing that the chain carries on
options.feedback: A bond through each bracket. Stopping it inside the bracket loses the mark.
The hydrogens stay on their carbons inside the brackets. What crosses the bracket is a bond.
n goes after the closing bracket, low down, not through it.
The double bond is gone once the chain forms. It is a single bond that crosses each bracket.

items.stem: Which atoms does one repeat unit of poly(chloroethene) contain?

options.text: 2 C, 3 H and 1 Cl, the same as chloroethene
options.feedback: The same atoms as the monomer, because nothing leaves when the monomers join.
That keeps all four of ethene's hydrogens and adds the chlorine too. The chlorine took one hydrogen's place.

options.text: 2 C, 2 H and 1 Cl, because a hydrogen leaves as the bond opens
options.feedback: Nothing leaves in addition polymerisation. Only a bond changes; every atom stays.
Chloroethene has one chlorine atom. The chlorine is not there as Cl₂.

items.stem: A polymer chain repeats the pattern –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–. Which monomer was it made from?
items.skill: Work back from a polymer to its monomer

options.feedback: Put the C=C back into one two-carbon unit and count all three carbons.
The double bond has to go back in. Propane has none, so it could not have made this chain.
Ethene would give CH₂ on both carbons. The CH₃ carbon counts too, making three.
Count again: two carbons in the chain plus the one in CH₃ make three, not four.

indicativeContent.point: The monomer is chloroethene, which is unsaturated: it has a C=C double bond.
Many monomers join to form one very long chain molecule, the polymer poly(chloroethene).
One of the two bonds in each C=C opens, and the spare bond on each carbon links to the next monomer.
Nothing else is formed, so the repeat unit has exactly the atoms of the monomer, C₂H₃Cl.
The repeat unit is drawn as two carbons joined by a single bond, with a bond passing through a bracket on each side.
n after the bracket shows the unit repeating many times; the drawing is checked by counting four bonds at every carbon.

scheme.for: a banded answer covering the monomer and its C=C, many monomers joining into a long chain, the name addition polymerisation, one bond of each C=C opening to link to the next monomer, no other product so the repeat unit has the monomer's atoms, and the repeat unit drawn with a single C–C bond, a bond through each bracket and n
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Monomer, process, what happens to the bond, then the drawing and its check.
Use the words addition polymerisation, repeat unit and double bond.
parts.workedSolution: The monomer is chloroethene, which is unsaturated because it has a C=C double bond. In addition polymerisation many of these monomers join to form one very long chain molecule, poly(chloroethene). One of the two bonds in each C=C opens, and the spare bond on each carbon links it to the next monomer, so the chain has only single bonds. Nothing else is formed, so the repeat unit contains exactly the atoms of the monomer, C2H3Cl. The repeat unit is drawn as two carbons joined by a single bond, carrying the chlorine and three hydrogens, with a bond passing through a square bracket on each side and n after the closing bracket to show that the unit repeats many times. It can be checked by counting four bonds at every carbon and the same atoms as the monomer.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife is asked: 'Ethene forms an addition polymer. Name the monomer and name the polymer. [2]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Polymer = poly(ethane), because the chain has only single bonds
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The monomer is right. The polymer's name is not built from what the chain looks like: it is built from the monomer's name. Poly, then ethene in brackets, gives poly(ethene), even though the chain itself has no double bonds.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the two marks. Naming the polymer from its monomer is a rule rather than chemistry to work out, which is why Summer 2025's report found it beyond most candidates. Learn it once: poly, then the monomer in brackets.

findTheMistake.stem: Conor is asked to draw the repeat unit of poly(ethene). He lists what his drawing shows:
studentWorking: Atoms on each carbon = two hydrogen atoms
Bond between the two carbons = double bond
Outer bonds = one through each bracket, with n after the closing bracket
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The double bond is the one thing that must not survive. It is what opened to make the chain. Kept, and with the bond through the bracket as well, each carbon would have five bonds, which carbon never has.
correction: Bond between the two carbons = single bond
Also accepted = the carbons are joined by a single bond
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the two marks: the brackets, the bonds through them and the n are all right. Count four bonds at every carbon before you move on; five means the double bond is still there.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked to name the monomer of a polymer whose chain repeats –CH₂–CHCl–.
Her working:
studentWorking: Repeat unit = two carbons, one CH2 and one CHCl
Remove the two bonds that joined the unit to its neighbours
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The first two steps are right, but the double bond was never put back. With only a single bond between them, each carbon would be a bond short. Restoring the C=C gives CH₂=CHCl, which is chloroethene, the monomer CCEA names.
correction: Also accepted = the monomer is chloroethene
findTheMistake.feedback: The unit was marked off correctly. The last step of working backwards is always the same: put the C=C back. A monomer for addition polymerisation must have one, so its name ends in -ene.
